claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy has a stable, single-phase microstructure.
The initial alloy is currently used as an intermediate material in plasma-facing reactor components.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 5 wt.% Cu to the HEA.
Approximately 5 wt.% Cu will enhance the alloy's electron-mediated thermal conductivity.
Approximately 5 wt.% Cu will preserve the alloy's single solid-solution phase.
A single solid-solution phase is key to the alloy's mechanical stability in a plasma-facing intermediate layer.
Cyclic thermal and mechanical loading at approximately 500–800°C is typical of plasma-facing applications.
Phase-diagram-inspired design approaches can predict whether HEAs form single solid-solution or composite phases.
Phase-diagram-guided design will ensure that the minor Cu addition does not trigger deleterious phase separation in the proposed alloy.
Copper has high electron-mediated thermal conductivity.
Adding Cu increases the density of conduction electrons in the HEA.
The Cu-induced increase in conduction-electron density improves electron-mediated heat transfer.
Guided compositional tuning preserves the alloy's structural integrity.
The Cu-doped HEA will have higher thermal conductivity than the undoped baseline.
The Cu-doped HEA will retain creep resistance and structural stability comparable to the undoped baseline under reactor-relevant thermal and mechanical loads.
The undoped standard HEA intermediate layer has moderate thermal conductivity and proven mechanical stability.
Exceeding the controlled Cu concentration could cause secondary-phase formation or degradation of mechanical properties.
Secondary-phase formation or mechanical degradation is especially likely above 800°C or under extreme stress.
